ADDITIONAL SESSIONS JUDGE-03, SOUTH EAST DISTRICT,
 SAKET COURTS, NEW DELHI
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
The present criminal revision petition has been preferred by the revisionist/complainant assailing the order dated 24.03.2025 passed by the Ld. Judicial Magistrate First Class-08, South East, Saket Courts (in Ct Cases 662/2022), whereby the complaint under Section 200 CrPC seeking summoning of the respondent for the offence under Section 420 IPC was dismissed.
2.

entities.text: Judicial Magistrate First Class-08, South East, Saket Courts
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
The revisionist has contended that the Ld. Trial Court failed to appreciate the material placed on record and that the testimony of CW-1 and CW-2 along with the Agreement to Sell clearly establishes that the respondent had entered into an agreement to sell the property for a Hamid Hussain vs Sherunisha on 1 April, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/110070117/
1 consideration of 5,50,000/- and had received part payment of 2,00,000/-.

It is further argued that despite receiving the said amount, the respondent neither handed over possession of the property nor honoured the terms of the agreement and the property was allegedly sold to a third person.
According to the revisionist, these facts disclose the commission of the offence of cheating and the Ld. Trial Court erred in treating the matter as a purely civil dispute.

Ld. Counsel for revisionist has relied upon the judgments of Lalita Kumar Vs. Govt of UP & Ors.
Crl Rev. No. 367 of 2025 Hamid Hussain Vs Sherunisha Page No. 2 of 8 (AIR 2014 Supreme Court 187) Hridaya Rangan Pd. Verma and Ors. Vs. State of Bihar and Anr. (AIR 2000 Supreme Court 2341) in support of his contentions.
3. Heard.

entities.text:
Lalita Kumar Vs. Govt of UP & Ors.
Crl Rev. No. 367 of 2025
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Hamid Hussain Vs Sherunisha Page No. 2 of 8 (AIR 2014 Supreme Court 187)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Hridaya Rangan Pd. Verma and Ors. Vs. State of Bihar and Anr. (AIR 2000 Supreme Court 2341)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Record perused.
4. Before proceeding further, it would be apt to recall the note of caution that was voiced by the Apex Court in M/s Pepsi Foods Ltd. vs. Special Judicial Magistrate, AIR 1998 SC 128.

entities.text: M/s Pepsi Foods Ltd. vs. Special Judicial Magistrate, AIR 1998 SC 128
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Apex Court held that summoning of an accused in a criminal case is a serious matter.

I t was observed as under:-
"Summoning of an accused in a criminal case is a serious matter.
Criminal law cannot be set into motion as a matter of course.
It is not that the complainant has to bring only two witnesses to support his allegations in the complaint to have the criminal law set into motion.
The order of the Magistrate summoning the accused must reflect that he has applied his mind to the facts of the case and the law applicable thereto.

He has to examine the nature of allegations made in the complaint and the evidence both oral and documentary in support thereof and that would be sufficient for the complainant to succeed in bringing charge home to the accused.
It is not that the Magistrate is a silent spectator at the time of recording of preliminary evidence before summoning of the accused.

Magistrate has to carefully scrutinize the evidence brought on record and may even himself put questions to the complainant and his witnesses to elicit answers to find out the truthfulness of the allegations or otherwise and then examine if any offence is prima facie committed by all or any of the accused".
5. Similar are the observations of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Ravindranatha Bajpe vs Mangalore Special Economic Zone Ltd. & Crl Rev. No. 367 of 2025 Hamid Hussain Vs Sherunisha Page No. 3 of 8 Others, Crl Appeal No.1047-1048/2021 dated 27th September 2021.
6.

entities.text: Ravindranatha Bajpe vs Mangalore Special Economic Zone Ltd. & Crl Rev. No. 367 of 2025
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Hamid Hussain Vs Sherunisha Page No. 3 of 8 Others
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In the instant case, the record reveals that the Ld. Magistrate had considered the testimony of the complainant and his witness as well as the document relied upon by the complainant, namely the agreement to sell.

The Ld. Magistrate also took into account the status report filed during the enquiry wherein it was stated that the proposed accused had claimed that the amount was returned to the complainant after withdrawal from her bank account when the deal could not be finalized.
7.

The primary question which arises for consideration is whether the material placed on record before the Ld. Magistrate disclosed the essential ingredients of the offence of cheating so as to justify Hamid Hussain vs Sherunisha on 1 April, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/110070117/
2 summoning of the respondent.

entities.text: Hamid Hussain vs Sherunisha on 1 April, 2026 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 8. For an offence under Section 420 IPC, it is well settled that the complainant must prima facie show that the accused had a dishonest or fraudulent intention at the very inception of the transaction.

Mere failure to honour a contractual obligation or subsequent breach of an agreement does not by itself constitute the offence of cheating unless it is shown that the accused had such dishonest intention from the very beginning.
9. In the present case, the material relied upon by the revisionist essentially relates to an agreement to sell and an alleged breach thereof.
Crl Rev. No. 367 of 2025 Hamid Hussain Vs Sherunisha Page No. 4 of 8
Even as per the evidence led during the pre-summoning stage, the complainant has only stated that the accused failed to hand over possession despite receiving part consideration.
10. The Ld. Magistrate, upon evaluating the material, rightly observed that there is nothing on record to indicate that the respondent had any dishonest intention at the inception of the transaction.
The dispute appears to arise out of an alleged non-performance of contractual obligations under an agreement to sell.

11. Further, in State of Kerala vs A. Pareed Pillai & Anr., AIR 1973 SC 326, the Supreme Court held that to hold a person guilty of the offence of cheating, it has to be shown that his intention was dishonest at the time of making the promise.

entities.text: State of Kerala vs A. Pareed Pillai & Anr., AIR 1973 SC 326
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Such dishonest intention cannot be inferred from the mere fact that he could not subsequently fulfill the promise.

12. If the present case is tested upon the principles of law as laid down by the Apex Court in the aforesaid cases, then it is evident that no offence for cheating or any other offence is made out in the present case and the act of the respondents can at the most be termed as breach of contract only.
In my view, the revisionist is having a grievance of not receiving his pending dues from the respondents and appears to have filed the criminal complaint for recovery of the same.
Failed obligation and frustrated expectations cannot give rise to any criminal liability.
Crl Rev. No. 367 of 2025 Hamid Hussain Vs Sherunisha Page No. 5 of 8 13.
Even superior courts have time and again deprecated the initiation of false criminal proceedings in cases having elements of civil disputes.
The quick relief offered by criminal prosecution as opposed to a civil dispute incentivizes litigants to initiate vexatious proceedings.

The Hon'ble Apex Court in G. Sagar Suri vs State of UP, Crl Appeal No. 91/2000 (28.01.2000) observed as under:
"It is to be seen if a matter, which is essentially of civil nature, has been given a cloak of criminal offence.

entities.text: G. Sagar Suri vs State of UP, Crl Appeal No. 91/2000 (28.01.2000)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Criminal proceedings are not a short cut of other remedies available in law.
Before issuing process a criminal court has to exercise a great deal of caution.
For the accused it is a serious matter.

This court has laid certain principles on the basis of which High Court is to exercise its jurisdiction under section 482 Hamid Hussain vs Sherunisha on 1 April, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/110070117/
3 Cr
. P.C. Jurisdiction under this section has to be exercised to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice".

14. Further, in case titled as M/s Indian Oil Corporation VS M/s NEPC India Ltd & Ors, in Appeal (Crl) No. 834/2002 date of judgment 20.07.2006, Hon'ble Apex court has observed as under:-
"While on this issue, it is necessary to take notice of a growing tendency in business circles to convert purely civil disputes into criminal cases.

entities.text: M/s Indian Oil Corporation VS M/s NEPC India Ltd & Ors
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: This is obviously on account of a prevalent impression that civil law remedies are time consuming and do not adequately protect the interests of lenders/creditors.
Such a tendency is seen in several family disputes also, leading to irretrievable break down of marriages/families.
There is also an impression that if a person could somehow be entangled in a criminal prosecution, there is a likelihood of imminent settlement.
Any effort to settle civil disputes and claims, which do not involve any criminal offence, by applying pressure though criminal prosecution should be deprecated and discouraged.

15. Applying the aforesaid principles to the facts of the present case, this Court finds that the allegations primarily disclose a dispute arising Crl Rev. No. 367 of 2025 Hamid Hussain Vs Sherunisha Page No. 6 of 8 out of an agreement to sell and the alleged failure to perform contractual obligations.

entities.text: Crl Rev. No. 367 of 2025 Hamid Hussain Vs Sherunisha Page No. 6 of 8
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Such a dispute is essentially civil in nature, for which the appropriate remedy lies before the competent civil court.
16. The Ld. Magistrate has examined the material placed on record and has given cogent reasons for concluding that the essential ingredients of the offence under Section 420 IPC are not made out.
The impugned order does not suffer from any illegality, impropriety or jurisdictional error warranting interference in revisional jurisdiction.
17. Accordingly, this Court finds no merit in the present revision petition.
18. In my considered view, the Ld. Trial Court was justified in dismissing the complaint of the revisionist.
Therefore, there is no illegality in the impugned order and the present petition is devoid of merit.

19. The revision petition is accordingly dismissed and the impugned order passed by the Ld. Judicial Magistrate First Class is affirmed.
20. TCR be sent back to the Ld. Trial Court along with a copy of this judgment.
Crl Rev. No. 367 of 2025 Hamid Hussain Vs Sherunisha Page No. 7 of 8 21.
Revision file be consigned to the Record Room after due compliance.
by ANUJ ANUJ
